questions.question: What is a 'golden dataset' used for in LLM evaluation?
options: Storing a model's most expensive API calls
A curated set of representative inputs paired with known-good expected outputs or scoring criteria, used to repeatably measure quality before deployment
A backup copy of the production database
A list of banned words for content moderation
questions.explanation: A golden dataset provides a consistent, repeatable benchmark to measure whether a prompt or model change improves, maintains, or regresses quality, compared to the current production version.

questions.question: Why do LLM evals need different techniques than traditional software testing's simple 'assert result == expected value'?
options: LLM evals don't actually need to be any different from traditional testing
LLM outputs are non-deterministic and often open-ended, so evals need approaches like rule-based scoring, LLM-as-judge, or human review rather than exact equality checks
LLM outputs are always identical, so testing is unnecessary
Traditional software testing never uses any scoring at all
questions.explanation: Because the same input can produce varying, open-ended outputs, evals need scoring methods (rule-based checks, LLM-as-judge, human review) suited to measuring quality on a spectrum, rather than a simple pass/fail equality test.

questions.question: A team changes a system prompt and someone asks whether it made quality better or worse, but the team has only done a few spot checks. Which question best identifies the missing capability?
options: Should we just trust the spot checks and move forward?
Do we have a golden dataset and repeatable scoring method to measure this change's actual impact on quality, rather than relying on a few manual spot checks?
Should we avoid ever changing prompts again to prevent this uncertainty?
Is this definitely not measurable in any way?
questions.explanation: This scenario is a direct symptom of missing eval infrastructure — a golden dataset with a repeatable scoring method turns 'did this help or hurt' from a guess into a measured, comparable result.
